To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

short‐laid geographical differences in the magnitude of wholesale gasoline price increases following a major hurricane are associated with longlaid geographical differences (i.e., differences that persist for more than 2 months) in retail prices.

short‐liven geographical differences in the size of wholesale gasoline price increases are associated with long-lasting geographical differences in retail gasoline prices, and that the long-lasting differences in retail prices are smaller in cities where there are more retail gasoline price cycles.
temporary differences in the severity and duration of wholesale gasoline price increases are associated with long-term differences in retail gasoline prices.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the retail gasoline market responds to short‐term price fluctuations at the wholesale level.
how the market characteristics of a city influence how it responds to shocks.
the impact of a hurricane on gasoline prices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
retail price cycles are an effective mechanism for transmitting wholesale price shocks to consumers.
the results are consistent with the hypothesis that the temporary wholesale price increases caused by Hurricane Rita led to long-lasting retail price increases in some areas.
the wholesale gasoline price spikes associated with Hurricane Rita were not fully passed through to consumers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
retail price cycles are a feature of markets that are less competitive.

temporary differences in the severity and duration of wholesale gasoline price fluctuations are associated with long-lasting geographical differences in retail margins, and that the magnitude of the latter depends in part on the extent to which retail competition is concentrated into large retail outlets.

temporary differences in the severity with which hurricanes disrupt wholesale supply are associated with long-lasting differences in retail prices that are driven in part by differences in the degree of competition among gasoline stations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the retail gasoline price cycle may be an important factor that determines how quickly retail margins fall following temporary wholesale price spikes.
the effects of temporary wholesale price shocks on retail prices can last for a long time, even in markets where competition among retailers is intense.
short‐term differences in wholesale prices can lead to long‐term differences in retail prices.
